details:
**Weighing of the heart against the Feather of Ma'at**
Anubis's most famous role: in the Hall of Two Truths, he weighs the heart of a dead person on a scale against the feather of Ma'at, goddess of truth and order, earning him the title "Guardian of the Scales." This judgment, depicted in the Book of the Dead, decides whether the soul may pass on to the afterlife (the Field of Reeds).

**Ammit**
The monstrous "Devourer of the Dead," with a crocodile's head, a lion's forequarters, and a hippopotamus's hindquarters. Ammit waits beside the scales during the weighing of the heart, and Anubis lets her eat the hearts of those who fail, destroying their souls, while protecting the innocent from her.

**Branding Set as a leopard**
While Anubis guarded Osiris's body, Set disguised himself as a leopard to attack or steal it. Anubis branded him all over with a hot iron rod, which explains the leopard's spots, and in some versions flayed Set and wore his skin, explaining why Anubis's priests wore leopard skins.

**Kebechet**
Anubis's daughter, a goddess of purification whose name means "cooling water." She was depicted as a serpent (sometimes with a star-studded body) and gave cool water to the spirits of the dead during embalming and in the afterlife.

**Son of Nephthys and Osiris**
In the best-known account, Nephthys disguised herself as her sister Isis to sleep with Osiris, and Anubis was born from this union; Isis later raised him. Other traditions name Set or Ra as his father, or other goddesses such as Bastet or Hesat as his mother.

**Opening of the Mouth ceremony**
A funerary ritual in which a priest wearing an Anubis mask touched the mouth of the mummy or a statue with ritual tools. It restored the dead person's ability to eat, drink, speak, and breathe in the afterlife (the Duat).

**Embalming Osiris and inventing mummification**
After Set killed Osiris, Anubis helped Isis embalm his body and wrapped it in linen to prevent decay, inventing mummification. This made Anubis the patron god of embalmers and cemeteries, and in one story he was given Osiris's organs.

**Jackal head**
Anubis is depicted as a man with the head of a black jackal or as a reclining black jackal (canine), likely because jackals scavenged around cemeteries. His black color symbolized the fertile Nile soil and rebirth, not evil.

**Psychopomp and identification with Hermes**
Anubis guided the souls of the dead into the Duat (underworld) and to Osiris for judgment. Because of this role as a psychopomp, Greeks and Romans identified him with Hermes, producing the combined god Hermanubis.

**Cynopolis**
The Greek name ("City of the Dog") of the city in Upper Egypt's 17th nome that was the center of Anubis's cult. His consort Anput was the personification of that nome.

**Imiut fetish**
A cult object associated with Anubis: a headless animal skin (often described as a feline or bull hide) tied to a pole standing in a pot. It was carried in processions and placed in tombs.

**The Tale of Two Brothers**
An Egyptian New Kingdom story whose elder brother, Anpu, shares Anubis's name. Anpu's wife falsely accuses his younger brother Bata of seduction; Bata cuts off his own genitals, which a catfish eats, to prove his innocence, and Anpu kills his wife. Later Anpu searches for years to find Bata's heart and revives him.

**Epithets ("He who is upon his mountain," "Lord of the sacred land," "First of the Westerners")**
Titles describing Anubis as the guardian of necropolises, which lay in the desert hills to the west. He was called "First of the Westerners" (Khenti-Amentiu) before Osiris took over that title, and was also called "Subduer of the Nine Bows," the traditional enemies of Egypt.

**Maa kheru ("true of voice") and the negative confession**
Before the weighing of the heart, the dead person recited the "negative confession," denying sins before 42 divine assessors. Those who passed the judgment were declared "maa kheru," meaning "true of voice" or justified.

**Wepwawet**
A jackal god whose name means "Opener of the Ways," who was often confused with Anubis and is sometimes called his son. The epithet "Opener of the Ways" is sometimes also applied to Anubis himself.
